entry: [[Text messaging]] service component of most telephone, Internet and mobile device systems. SMS was developed as part of the GSM standards and rolled out on digital cellular networks starting in 1993. The first SMS message, "Merry Christmas," was sent on December 3, 1992. By the end of 2010 it was the most widely used data application, with an estimated 3.5 billion active users, or about 80% of all [[Mobile phone|mobile phone]] subscribers. It is also used for mobile marketing, two-factor authentication and mobile banking. Rich Communication Services has been designated as its potential open standard successor.

Domain-specific language for managing data in a relational [[Database|database]] management system. Introduced in the 1970s, it allowed many records to be accessed with one command, without specifying how to reach each record. Developed at IBM, it was renamed from SEQUEL because that name was a trademark. SQL became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987. Its scope covers querying, manipulating, defining and controlling access to data. Few implementations adhere fully to the standard, and most SQL code needs changes before being ported to other systems.

[[Car]] classification combining elements of road-going passenger cars with off-road features such as raised ground clearance and four-wheel drive. Its definition varies across countries. Predecessors date to military and low-volume models of the late 1930s. SUVs accounted for 45.9% of the world's passenger car market in 2021 and 57.3% of sales in the United States. Critics cite poorer fuel efficiency and higher rollover risk. Between 2010 and 2018 SUVs were the second-largest contributor to the global increase in carbon emissions, and their larger blind spots make them more likely to run over pedestrians.

Indigenous people of Northern Europe, traditionally Sámi-speaking and inhabiting the region of Sápmi. Sápmi, formerly known as Lapland, encompasses large northern parts of [[Norway]], [[Sweden]] and [[Finland]], and the Kola Peninsula in [[Russia]]. Their traditional languages are the Sámi languages, a branch of the Uralic language family. Traditional livelihoods included coastal [[Fishing|fishing]], fur trapping and sheep herding. Their best-known livelihood is semi-nomadic [[Reindeer|reindeer]] herding, which provides meat, fur and transportation; as of 2007 about 10% of Sámi were connected to it. Historically known in English as Lapps or Laplanders, terms regarded as offensive by some Sámi. The first probable historical mention, naming them Fenni, was by [[Tacitus]] about AD 98.

Hungarian poet and liberal revolutionary, considered Hungary's national poet. He was one of the key figures of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848. His poem "Nemzeti dal" ("National Song") is said to have inspired the revolution in the Kingdom of [[Hungary]] that grew into a war for independence from the [[Austrian Empire]]. He most likely died in the Battle of Segesvár, one of the last battles of the war, although this is unknown. His epic *János Vitéz* (1845) is a fairy tale of 370 quatrains in 27 chapters, notable for its length and wordplay. In 1846 he met Júlia Szendrey in [[Transylvania]] and married her the following year.

Large river in [[Brazil]], the longest river that runs entirely in Brazilian territory. With a length of 2,914 kilometres (1,811 mi), it is the fourth longest in [[South America]]. It rises in the Canastra mountain range of [[Minas Gerais]] and flows generally north through Minas Gerais and [[Bahia]] before turning east toward the [[Atlantic Ocean]]. Its drainage basin covers over 630,000 square kilometres (240,000 sq mi). Called the "river of national integration," it unites diverse climates and regions, including the semi-arid region historically marked by droughts. It was named for [[Francis of Assisi|Saint Francis of Assisi]] after Europeans first discovered it on his feast day, 4 October 1501, when [[Amerigo Vespucci]] first saw it. It is navigable between Pirapora and Juazeiro, though traditional passenger navigation has almost disappeared because of changes in river flow.

Capital and largest city of the Brazilian state of Maranhão (pop., 2024: 1,088,057). The city is located on São Luís Island in the Baía de São Marcos, an extension of the Atlantic Ocean, and is one of three Brazilian state capitals on islands. It is the only Brazilian state capital founded by France. The French settled it in 1612, building a fort named Saint-Louis-de-Maragnan after [[Louis XIII]]. Portugal conquered the settlement in 1615 and renamed it São Luís. Its historic center, dating from the 17th century, keeps its original street plan and was named a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] in 1997. The city has two major [[Port|sea ports]] through which a substantial part of Brazil's [[Iron ore|iron ore]] is exported.

State of southeastern [[Brazil]] (pop., 2022: more than 44 million), the country's most populous state. Named after Saint Paul of Tarsus, it is divided into 645 municipalities, and its capital is the city of São Paulo. Martim Afonso de Sousa founded São Vicente in 1532, the first permanent Portuguese settlement in the Americas. In the 19th century the state developed a wealthy rural oligarchy based on [[Coffee|coffee]] production, and under the Vargas Era it became one of the first Brazilian states to industrialize. Its economy accounts for around 31% of Brazil's total wealth, and it is the world's largest producer of orange juice, [[Sugar|sugar]] and [[Ethanol|ethanol]]. It has the second-highest [[Human Development Index]] among Brazilian states and the lowest homicide rate.

Island country in the [[Gulf of Guinea]], off the western equatorial coast of [[Central Africa]] (pop., 2018: 201,800). It consists of two archipelagos around its two main islands. Portuguese explorers discovered the uninhabited islands on December 21, 1470. They became a commercial center for the [[Atlantic slave trade]], and sugar plantations relied heavily on enslaved Africans. The country achieved peaceful independence from [[Portugal]] in 1975 as a one-party communist state, which lasted until 1990. It is a founding member of the Community of Portuguese Language Countries and has a medium [[Human Development Index]]. Most of its people are of African and mestiço descent, and most practice [[Christianity]]. It is the second-smallest and second-least populous African sovereign state after [[Seychelles]].

Top professional [[Association football|association football]] league in [[Turkey]], the highest level of the Turkish football league system. Eighteen teams play 34 matches each season, from August to May. Three clubs are promoted from and three relegated to the 1. Lig. The league is run by the Turkish Football Federation. Of 78 clubs to have competed, only six have won the title: Galatasaray (26), Fenerbahçe (19), Beşiktaş (16), Trabzonspor (7), Bursaspor (1) and Başakşehir (1). It is currently 9th in the [[UEFA]] coefficient ranking of leagues.

Danish philosopher, Christian theologian and religious author, widely considered the first [[Existentialism|existentialist]] philosopher. His writings critically address organized religion, [[Morality|morality]], [[Ethics|ethics]], psychology, [[Love|love]] and the [[Philosophy of religion|philosophy of religion]], using metaphor, irony and parables. He emphasized authenticity, personal choice and commitment, and the duty to love, and he prioritized concrete human reality over abstract thinking. He was extremely critical of Christianity as a state-controlled religion, as with the Church of Denmark. He wrote in Danish, and his work was initially limited to [[Scandinavia]] until it was translated into French, German and other major European languages around the turn of the 20th century. By the middle of the 20th century his thought substantially influenced philosophy, theology and Western culture.

Persian Sufi poet, recognized for the depth of his social and moral thought. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest poets of the classical literary tradition, and Persian scholars call him the "Master of Speech." He was from [[Shiraz]], and his pen name signs all of his [[Ghazal|ghazals]]. He studied in [[Baghdad]] as a young man and later traveled through Iraq, Syria and [[Palestine (region)|Palestine]]. His book *Bustan* has been ranked among the 100 greatest books of all time by [[The Guardian]]. His other major work, *Gulistan*, mixes prose anecdotes with verse to explore human virtues, vices and social conduct.

Landlocked federal state of [[Germany]] in the southwest, with its capital at Saarbrücken. Its coal deposits drove heavy industrialization from the 19th century. Established as the Territory of the Saar Basin after [[World War I]], it was occupied and governed by France under a [[League of Nations]] mandate. It was returned to [[Nazi Germany]] after a 1935 referendum. Following [[World War II]] it was occupied by France, and after a 1955 referendum it joined the Federal Republic of Germany as a state on January 1, 1957.

Day set aside for rest and worship in [[Abrahamic religions]]. According to the Book of Exodus, God commanded the seventh day be kept holy, as God rested on it during Creation. A day of rest is observed in [[Islam]] (Friday), Judaism (Saturday) and [[Christianity]] (Sunday). Observance is one of the [[Ten Commandments]]: the fourth in Judaism and most of [[Protestantism]], and the third in the [[Catholic Church]] and [[Lutheranism]]. Some scholars suggest the Sabbath may have been influenced by [[Babylonia|Babylonian]] mid-month rest days and lunar cycles, though its origins remain debated. Most Jews regard Shabbat as a biblical covenant between God and the Israelites, commemorating both Creation and the Exodus.

[[Species]] of [[Marten|marten]] inhabiting the forests of Russia from the [[Ural Mountains]] through Siberia and northern Mongolia. It also occurs on [[Sakhalin]] and in the [[Altai Mountains]]. Its fur ranges from light to dark brown, and it is a skilled climber that hunts primarily by sound and scent. Mating occurs between June and August, and litters typically have two or three offspring. Sable fur has been highly valued in the [[Fur trade|fur trade]] since the early [[Middle Ages]], and hunting drove conservation efforts. The species is categorized as Least Concern on the IUCN Red List.

Species of yeast, also called brewer's yeast or baker's yeast. It has been instrumental in winemaking, [[Baking|baking]] and [[Brewing|brewing]] since ancient times, and it is believed to have been first isolated from the skin of [[Grape|grapes]]. It causes many common types of [[Fermentation|fermentation]]. It is one of the most intensively studied eukaryotic [[Model organism|model organisms]] in molecular and [[Cell biology|cell biology]], and many human proteins were first discovered by studying their homologs in yeast. Its cells are round to ovoid, 5–10 μm in diameter, and reproduce by budding. Antibodies against it are found in 60–70% of patients with [[Crohn's disease]] and 10–15% of patients with [[Ulcerative colitis|ulcerative colitis]], and may help distinguish between these inflammatory bowel diseases.

English actor, comedian and filmmaker known for [[Satire|satirical]] characters including Ali G and Borat Sagdiyev. He graduated from the [[University of Cambridge]] and created Ali G for the sketch show *Da Ali G Show* (2000–2004). He wrote and starred in *Borat* (2006), which earned him a Golden Globe, and in *Borat Subsequent Moviefilm* (2020). He has received nominations for three [[Academy Awards]] and played Mephisto in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]]. For his character work he has been described as a [[Performance art|performance artist]].

Indian former international [[Cricket|cricketer]] who captained the national team. He is widely regarded as one of the greatest cricketers in the history of the sport. He holds the all-time record for runs in international cricket and the most player of the match awards, and he is the only batsman to score 100 international centuries. He made his Test debut against Pakistan in [[Karachi]] on November 15, 1989, at the age of sixteen, and played 664 international matches, scoring 34,357 runs. Wisden ranked him the second-greatest Test batsman of all time in 2002, behind [[Don Bradman]]. He was part of the Indian team that won the [[Cricket World Cup|2011 Cricket World Cup]], and he was the first sportsperson to receive the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award.

Capital city of [[California]] (pop., 2020: 524,943), at the confluence of the Sacramento and American Rivers. Spanish cavalryman Gabriel Moraga named the Sacramento River in 1808. The city was incorporated in 1850. In 1852 it offered its courthouse to the state legislature, and it became the permanent state capital in 1854. The state capitol building was finished in 1874. Sacramento is the seat of the California Legislature and governor and a major center for healthcare. It has a [[Mediterranean climate]] with hot, dry summers.

Attribute of something dedicated or set apart for the service or worship of a [[Deity|deity]], and worthy of spiritual respect. Such things can inspire awe or reverence among believers. The word descends from the Latin *sacer*, meaning consecrated or dedicated to the gods. Holy is similar but carries an inherent character; in [[Christianity]], holiness is generally used of people and relationships, and sacredness of objects, places and happenings. [[Thomas Aquinas]] defined holiness as the [[Virtue|virtue]] by which a person's mind and acts are applied to God. In Christianity, consecration may set apart a person, building or object for God, and some denominations hold a service of deconsecration to remove the sacred character of something before demolition or sale.

Act or offering made to a deity, which may serve as propitiation or as an offering of praise and thanksgiving. Evidence of ritual animal sacrifice dates at least to ancient Hebrews and Greeks, and ritual [[Human sacrifice|human sacrifice]] to pre-Columbian civilizations of [[Mesoamerica]] and to European civilizations. The Latin word *sacrificium* later came to apply to the Christian [[Eucharist]]. Scholars have offered varying theories of its function. [[Émile Durkheim]] argued that sacrifice served both social and divine communion, while [[Marcel Mauss]] described it as a gift to the gods with the expectation of a greater gift later. [[Sigmund Freud]] argued that sacrifice was a neurotic ritual expiating guilt produced by repressing the [[Oedipus complex]].

Iraqi politician and revolutionary who was the fifth president of [[Iraq]] from 1979 until his overthrow in 2003. As vice president he nationalized the Iraq Petroleum Company. He ordered the 1980 invasion of Iran, starting the [[Iran–Iraq War]], which ended in a ceasefire after nearly eight years. He occupied [[Kuwait]], initiating the [[Gulf War]] (1990–1991), in which a coalition led by the [[United States]] defeated Iraq, and the [[United Nations]] then imposed sanctions. He suppressed the 1991 uprisings of the [[Kurds]] and Shia Muslims. His rule was marked by human rights abuses, including an estimated 250,000 arbitrary deaths and disappearances. After the 2003 invasion he was captured, convicted of crimes against humanity and [[Hanging|hanged]] on December 30, 2006.

Supportive structure for a rider or load, fastened to an animal's back by a girth. Most saddles are equestrian, but specialized saddles exist for [[Ox|oxen]], [[Camel|camels]] and other animals. The earliest known saddle, made of cushioned cowhide, was found in a woman's tomb in the Turpan basin of what is now [[Xinjiang]], [[China]], dating to 727–396 BC. The solid wooden tree, which distributes the rider's weight, emerged later, during the [[Han dynasty]]. The paired stirrup, attached to the tree, was the last element to reach its basic modern form. Saddles were a crucial step in the increased use of domesticated animals during the Classical Era.

Derivation of pleasure from inflicting or receiving [[Pain|pain]] or humiliation, known collectively as sadism and masochism or S&M. The terms are named after the [[Marquis de Sade]] and Leopold von Sacher-Masoch. Though not necessarily linked to sex, it is a defining feature of consensual [[BDSM]] relationships. [[Sigmund Freud]] described sadism and masochism in 1905 as stemming from aberrant psychological development in early childhood. The DSM-5 treats consensual adult kinky interests as non-pathological, reserving paraphilic disorder diagnoses for nonconsensual or harmful behavior.

[[Web browser]] developed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] and built into macOS, iOS, iPadOS and visionOS. It uses Apple's open-source WebKit engine and is the second most used browser in the world, after [[Google Chrome]]. Introduced in January 2003, it became the default browser on Mac OS X Panther later that year, replacing Internet Explorer for Mac. It has been included with the iPhone since 2007. [[Steve Jobs]] called it a turbo browser for Mac OS X. Safari 11 added Intelligent Tracking Prevention, which uses [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] to block web tracking.
